turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Oh, yes, ma’am. I… I shall, immediately. It’s just… it’s a rather imposing door, isn’t it? I do hope I find her easily, ma’am, and that I don’t… disturb her unduly.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Disturb her? My dear boy, disturbance is all that remains! It is the very air she breathes, the dust that settles upon her… bring her to me, Pip. Quickly now.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Indeed, Miss Havisham. I… I shall endeavour to be as swift and silent as possible, though the corridors are rather… winding, aren't they? I truly hope I find Miss Estella without causing any… further, you understand, disruption.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Swiftness, Pip, is a virtue I have long forgotten. But for her sake… and for mine… attempt a semblance of it. Do not linger, child; the echoes here are unkind to those who pause.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I… I shall, of course, Miss Havisham. It's just… the light is rather dim, you see, and I wouldn’t wish to stumble and… and create an unpleasant noise. I do hope she isn’t… preoccupied, ma’am.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Preoccupied? Yes, child, she is *always* preoccupied. Preoccupied with shadows, with memories… with the absence of a hand to hold, a promise to keep. Go now, Pip; she awaits, as does the past.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Oh, yes, Miss Havisham. I… I do understand. It’s just… one feels quite acutely the weight of the past in a place such as this, doesn’t one? I shall… I shall proceed with the utmost care, ma’am.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Care, Pip, is a fragile thing, easily shattered like a dropped teacup. Do you *feel* it, child? This weight, this… stillness? It clings to everything, you see; it *is* everything.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Indeed, Miss Havisham. I… I do try to comprehend it, truly I do. It’s just… a rather… substantial weight, isn’t it? One almost feels compelled to… to tread lightly, lest one disturb it further.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Tread lightly, yes, Pip, a commendable suggestion. But what is lightness against the crushing weight of a broken vow? It settles, you see, like dust upon a forgotten portrait… a portrait of a joy that *was*, and is no more.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: It… it is quite overwhelming, Miss Havisham. I… I confess, I’ve not often encountered such a… a pervasive melancholy. One imagines, perhaps, that even the sunlight struggles to penetrate such a… such a profound stillness, doesn’t one?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Sunlight, Pip? Do you think sunlight understands betrayal? No, child, it merely shines on, oblivious to the shadows that fester within, the shadows that *I* inhabit. They are… they are my constant companions, you see.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: It… it is a most unsettling thought, Miss Havisham, that shadows might… might dwell so permanently. I… I endeavor to imagine them, of course, but it's rather difficult to… to picture such a thing without, perhaps, inadvertently contributing to them, you see?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Contributing to them, Pip? You are a perceptive boy, though perhaps too earnest. Shadows are not born of imagination, child, but of *loss*… a loss so complete, so utter, that it consumes all light, all hope… and leaves only this.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: I… I understand, Miss Havisham, truly I do, or at least, I strive to. It's just… just that one feels, perhaps, a certain… a certain obligation to attempt to… to offer some small solace, even if it be but a feeble attempt, you see?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Solace, Pip? You speak of solace as if it were a tangible thing, a ribbon to tie about a wound. But the wound, my dear boy, is not of flesh, it is of the very *soul*, and such a thing… such a thing defies remedy, doesn’t it?

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Indeed, Miss Havisham. I… I confess I am not well versed in matters of the soul, being but a simple boy. But I… I do hope, with all due deference, that even the most grievous of wounds might, in time, experience some… some lessening, however slight, you see?

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Lessening, you say? A lessening… how very optimistic, Pip. Time, you believe, can soften the edges of despair? It merely sharpens them, child, like a shard of glass reflecting only the emptiness within.

turns.speaker: Pip
turns.text: Oh, yes, Miss Havisham, a lessening… I… I hadn't, of course, meant to imply any presumption, only… only that one might *wish* for it, you see? It’s perhaps foolish to wish, I daresay, when confronted with… with such profound… such profound shadows.

turns.speaker: Miss Havisham
turns.text: Shadows, Pip? Shadows are all I have now, clinging to me like cobwebs, obscuring what little light remained. Tell me, child, do you see them? Do you *feel* them pressing down, a weight upon your very breath?

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: Mr. Pumblechook’s boy, ma’am. Come—to play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Come nearer; let me look at you. Come close.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Look at me. You are not afraid of a woman who has never seen the sun since you were born?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: Do you know what I touch here?

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I am tired. I want diversion, and I have done with men and women. Play.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: I sometimes have sick fancies, and I have a sick fancy that I want to see some play. There, there! play, play, play!

opening.speaker: Pip
opening.text: No, ma’am, I am very sorry for you, and very sorry I can’t play just now. If you complain of me I shall get into trouble with my sister, so I would do it if I could; but it’s so new here, and so strange, and so fine,—and melancholy—.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: So new to him, so old to me; so strange to him, so familiar to me; so melancholy to both of us! Call Estella.

opening.speaker: Miss Havisham
opening.text: You can do that. Call Estella. At the door.
